analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.77 per hour over three years.
analysis.headline: The minimum wage bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have lifted the federal minimum wage in three steps: to $5.65 an hour on enactment, $6.15 a year later, and $6.77 two years after that, for an overall increase of $1.62 an hour. The federal minimum wage had been stuck at $5.15 since 1997. The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, later sent to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum, who would see their hourly pay rise by up to $1.62 over three years, and the low-income households that depend on those wages.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.65 within 90 days of enactment, then to $6.15 a year later and $6.77 two years after that.
The federal minimum wage had not been raised since 1997, so a $1.62 increase would have been the first boost to minimum-wage paychecks in roughly four years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay at or near the minimum wage, chiefly restaurants, retail stores, and other small and large businesses, which would face higher payroll costs; some of that cost may be passed to consumers through prices or offset through reduced hiring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Employers, especially small restaurants and retailers, would face higher payroll costs, and honest supporters acknowledge that some businesses respond by raising prices, reducing hours, or cutting entry-level jobs.
A nationwide $6.77 floor applies the same rate to high-cost cities and low-cost rural areas alike, which can bite hardest in places where living costs and prevailing wages are already low.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For minimum-wage workers, a 31% raise over three years is substantial and direct; for businesses, the cost is real but phased in over three years, which softens the shock. The trade-off is the standard one for minimum wage policy: higher pay for the lowest earners against somewhat higher costs for employers and possible modest effects on entry-level hiring.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which passed it along to a subcommittee, and it never received a hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the bill on June 28, 2001.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On March 19, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill ended the 107th Congress with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the minimum wage kept the wage at $5.15 an hour, while minimum-wage workers received no increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; workers got no raise

for.name: Rep. James Traficant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the minimum wage by $1.62 over three years; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: House committee of referral (chaired by Rep. John Boehner, R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it referred the bill to a subcommittee, where it died.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of the issue never showed up in the record on this bill.

industries.note: Would have faced higher wage bills for tipped and entry-level staff under a higher federal floor; the industry's interest in keeping the wage at $5.15 ran against workers' paychecks.
Large numbers of minimum-wage workers in retail would have meant significant payroll cost increases, offset partly by higher consumer spending from those workers.
